title: Land That Feeds a Continent Must Be Free to Travel
imageAlt: A woman holding freshly harvested millet in a Sahel field at sunset, a truck on the road behind
description: In the Sahel, a woman harvests millet from a field that ten years ago was bare ground. Further south, in a market in Lagos or Abidjan, families pay more each month for food that has crossed an ocean.
body: In the Sahel, a woman harvests millet from a field that ten years ago was bare ground. Further south, in a market in Lagos or Abidjan, families pay more each month for food that has crossed an ocean. Between that field and that market, distance is not the main obstacle. What separates them is a border post, a missing road, a standard that is not recognised on the other side, a cold store that was never built.

For two decades, Africa has invested its political will in restoring land. That work matters, and it is bearing fruit: soils are returning, farmers are coming back, communities are staying. But restored land answers only half of the question. The other half is what happens to the harvest once it leaves the field.

A sorghum surplus in one country should meet a shortage in another. Too often it does not. It rots in storage, sells at a loss in a saturated local market, or is never planted at all, because the farmer knows there is no buyer within reach. Today, trade between African countries still accounts for only around 16 percent of the continent's total trade. Most of what we eat travels a long way to reach us, while what we grow struggles to travel a short way.
Food moves when four conditions are met.

list.lead: Corridors that work for perishable goods:
list.text: roads, rail and border crossings where a truck of onions does not wait for days.
A tomato certified safe in Niger should be accepted as safe in Nigeria. Harmonised sanitary and quality rules do more for farmers than many subsidies.
Drying, milling, packaging and cold storage near the fields keep value in rural areas, create work for young people and allow goods to travel.

list.lead: Finance that reaches small producers and traders,
list.text: who carry most of the continent's food but rarely qualify for credit.

body: None of this is new thinking. What is new is that the instruments now exist to act on it at scale.

A country that cannot feed itself negotiates from a position of weakness. Every shock elsewhere, a war, a pandemic, a disruption to shipping, reaches African tables as a rise in prices. A continent that grows its own food and trades it within its own borders is not closing itself to the world. It meets the world on firmer ground. Food sovereignty is not self-isolation. It is the ability to choose.

Africa has already done the hardest part: it has agreed. On one side, the Great Green Wall has grown from a Sahelian ambition into a continental commitment to restore land. On the other, fifty African states have ratified the agreement creating a single continental market. These are two of the most important decisions our leaders have taken in a generation.

The work ahead is to bring them together. Restored land should be seen as the supply base of the continental market, and the continental market as the outlet that makes restoration pay. When a farmer in the Sahel knows her harvest can reach a buyer two borders away, she plants more, invests more and stays on her land. That is how restoration becomes an economy, and how an economy becomes resilience.

body.closing: The land is coming back. Now it must be free to travel.

title: The Second Chapter: Making Our Agreements Live
imageAlt: A woman trader carrying goods through a West African border crossing at dawn
description: In March 2018, in Kigali, African leaders put their signatures to an agreement that many observers had said could not be written.
body: In March 2018, in Kigali, African leaders put their signatures to an agreement that many observers had said could not be written. Countries with different currencies, legal systems, languages and economic structures agreed to build a single market. Today, fifty of them have ratified it.

It is worth pausing on what that required. Negotiation among sovereign states is slow and demanding work. Every concession had to be explained at home, to ministries, to industries, to citizens who wanted to know what they would gain. The leaders and negotiators who carried this process did the hardest part of integration: they turned an old aspiration into a binding commitment. Africa owes them that.

The same can be said of other continental commitments. The Great Green Wall began as a Sahelian vision and has become a continental objective. The Single African Air Transport Market set out to open African skies to African airlines. Each was an act of political courage, taken with full knowledge that the results would come slowly.

Every great agreement has two chapters. The first is written in conference halls, in legal texts, in the language of articles and annexes. The second is written somewhere else entirely: at a border post at dawn, in a customs office, in the accounts of a small business deciding whether to sell to a neighbouring country.

The second chapter is less visible, and it rarely makes the news. But it is the one citizens will remember. A woman trader does not read the protocol on rules of origin. She knows whether her goods crossed the border in an hour or in three days.
In the work I have been part of across eleven African countries, restoring land and building livelihoods around it, a few lessons have come back again and again.

list.text: Governors, mayors, traditional leaders and community organisations make or unmake any continental ambition. They need to be partners from the first day, not informed on the last.
Land restoration, like trade infrastructure, pays back over years. Finance that expects returns within a quarter will not build a corridor or a cooperative.

list.lead: The private sector must be a partner, not a spectator.
list.text: Businesses are not only the beneficiaries of integration. They are the ones who make it real, every time they buy, sell, hire and invest across a border.

body: None of this is a judgement on what has been done. It is simply the nature of the second chapter: it calls for different skills than the first.

The success of the second chapter will be measured in ordinary moments. A trader who crosses a border with one document instead of six. A young entrepreneur in Lagos who sells a digital service in Nairobi and Dakar without three separate licences. A cooperative that ships processed mango to a neighbouring country rather than raw fruit to another continent. A family that flies from one African capital to another without connecting through Europe.
These moments are already happening, and in growing numbers. The task now is to make them ordinary.

African integration is not a project that starts again with each generation. It is built in layers. The founders laid the foundations and wrote the rules, in difficult conditions and against a great deal of scepticism. The work ahead is to carry those rules into daily life, patiently, country by country and sector by sector.

body.closing: The texts exist. Their authors have done their part. The second chapter belongs to all of us.

title: What Holds When Everything Else Shakes
imageAlt: Old handwritten manuscripts kept in a metal trunk, lit by a lantern
description: In 2012, when armed groups occupied Timbuktu, the families of the city did something no army could have ordered. Night after night, they packed manuscripts into rice sacks and metal trunks, loaded them onto carts, boats and buses, and carried them south to Bamako.
body: In 2012, when armed groups occupied Timbuktu, the families of the city did something no army could have ordered. Night after night, they packed manuscripts into rice sacks and metal trunks, loaded them onto carts, boats and buses, and carried them south to Bamako. Hundreds of thousands of pages, some of them centuries old, on astronomy, law, medicine and poetry, crossed checkpoints hidden among ordinary goods. Most of them survived.
Nobody paid these families to take that risk. They took it because, to them, the manuscripts were not objects. They were the proof of who they were.

The mausoleums of Timbuktu, destroyed during the same occupation, were rebuilt a few years later by the city's own masons, using techniques handed down in their families for generations. I was Mali's Minister of Culture in those years. What I remember most is not the ceremonies. It is the masons, and the quiet pride of a city rebuilding with its own hands what had been taken from it.

body.heading: Culture is not what comes after

body: In times of crisis, culture is often treated as something for later. Security first, then the economy, and culture when calm returns. Experience teaches the opposite. When institutions weaken and markets close, it is culture that keeps a society standing: its languages, its music, its places of memory, its ways of settling disputes and welcoming strangers. It is what allows a community to recognise itself, and therefore to rebuild.

This is why the destruction of heritage is never an accident of war. Those who attack mausoleums and libraries know exactly what they are aiming at. In 2016, for the first time, the International Criminal Court tried a case centred on the destruction of cultural heritage, concerning Timbuktu, and handed down a conviction. The world had come to understand what the families of Timbuktu already knew.

In March 2017, at the Louvre, I spoke for Mali at the launch of an international alliance to protect heritage in conflict areas. The conviction in that room was simple: protecting heritage is not only a cultural policy. It is a security policy, and a development policy.

Africa holds one of the richest cultural heritages on earth, and one of the least protected. Its music fills stadiums on every continent. Its cinema, fashion, literature and design are followed and imitated far beyond its borders. Its historic cities, from Timbuktu to Lalibela to Kilwa, tell a story of learning, trade and faith that the world is only beginning to rediscover.
This is a world-class asset, and it deserves to be managed as one.

list.text: Inventories, archives, trained conservators, and local guardians who are recognised and supported in their role.
Musicians, artisans, filmmakers and designers need finance, protection of their rights and access to audiences, like any other industry.
A young African who knows the history of her own city carries a confidence that no imported curriculum can give.

body: We speak a great deal today about resilience: climate resilience, economic resilience, social resilience. All of them rest on something we rarely measure: the confidence of a people in its own story. A community that knows where it comes from bends without breaking. It rebuilds faster, because it knows what it is rebuilding.

body.closing: The families of Timbuktu understood this without needing a report to tell them. When everything else was shaking, they saved what would allow them to stand again.

title: Start With What They Already Know
imageAlt: A young woman sewing patterned fabric at a machine in a tailoring workshop
description: Somewhere in West Africa, a young woman completes a two-year tailoring apprenticeship. She can cut, sew and finish a garment to a standard any boutique would accept.
body: Somewhere in West Africa, a young woman completes a two-year tailoring apprenticeship. She can cut, sew and finish a garment to a standard any boutique would accept. She has her certificate. Then nothing happens. She has no machine of her own, no access to credit, no buyer beyond her neighbourhood. A year later, her skills are still there. Her confidence is not.

Her story is repeated across the continent, in workshops, vocational schools and training centres. We often ask what young Africans should be taught. It is a fair question, but it is often the wrong one to ask first. Many have already been taught. The real question is what happens the day after the training ends.

Training without capital produces plans, not businesses. Between a skill and a livelihood lie steps that no classroom covers: an honest assessment of readiness, a first contract, a small loan or grant, access to buyers, and someone to call when the first month goes wrong. When these steps are missing, talent waits. When they are in place, one trained person can become an employer.

Africa's young people are not a problem to be managed. A great many of them already work, often in the informal economy, with skills learned outside any institution: in the workshop of a master craftsman, at the market, in a phone repair stall, on a farm. These skills are real. What they need is to be verified and recognised, not taught again from the beginning.

For years, success has too often been counted in the number of people trained. That number says little about lives changed. Better questions are simple: how many people now earn a stable income? How many businesses are still open after two years? How many jobs have they created for others?

Measuring transformation rather than participation changes the behaviour of everyone involved: funders, training institutions, employers and governments. It moves attention from the classroom to the marketplace, which is where young people's futures are decided.

The goal is not one job for each young person. It is a young person who hires. A tailor with her own workshop takes on three apprentices. A mechanic who gets his first equipment loan employs two assistants within a year. The same logic applies to the land: restored landscapes create work in nurseries, processing, storage and transport, if trained people are connected to it.

body.text: This is the conviction behind Advance Africa, a human capital initiative connected to the Great Green Wall Foundation of Africa. Its approach is direct: start with people who are already trained, assess them, place them, finance them, and accompany them until they earn and employ others.

body.closing: Africa's young people have done their part. They have learned. Our part is to make sure that what they have learned leads somewhere.
